concept.name: Accrued interest
concept.definition: Interest earned on a security but not yet paid to the investor; specifically, the portion of the next coupon payment that has accumulated since the last coupon date, which a bond buyer pays to the seller at settlement.
concept.intuition: Coupons arrive only on payment dates, but interest builds every day: accrued interest is the seller's share of the coming coupon for the days they held the bond.
concept.mechanics: Accrued interest = coupon payment x (days since last coupon / days in coupon period), using the market's day-count convention (e.g., 30/360 for U.S. corporates, actual/actual for Treasuries). The buyer compensates the seller at settlement, then collects the full coupon on the next payment date; it is also an explicit component of futures invoice prices for deliverable bonds.
concept.formula: AI = C x (d / D), where C = periodic coupon payment, d = days from last coupon date to settlement, D = days in the coupon period (per the applicable day-count convention).
concept.failure_modes: Accrued interest depends on day-count conventions that differ across bond markets, so a single formula applied across markets miscalculates settlement amounts; it also creates small cash-flow mismatches when hedging coupon-paying bonds with derivatives.
concept.misconceptions: Accrued interest is not an extra cost or fee: the buyer effectively recovers it in the next full coupon payment, so it is a transfer, not an expense, though it does affect cash outlay at settlement.
concept.example: Buying a $1,000 bond with a 6% annual coupon (semiannual $30) exactly one-third of the way through the coupon period means paying about $10 of accrued interest to the seller on top of the quoted price.
